# Research notes on Ezekiel 8

**What I couldn't find.** I could only partly read two key pages. The Enduring Word page cut off partway through v. 14, so my notes on vv. 15–18 from that site come from search snippets only. The Precept Austin page cut off at v. 11. I found no pages from oca.org, newadvent.org, bibleodyssey.org, 1517.org, lcms.org or seedbed.com on this chapter. I also found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on it. The Catholic views below come only through older commentators who quote Jerome and the Vulgate (the Latin Bible). Wesley's Notes shows up on StudyLight only as a link, so I have no Wesleyan content. I found no case where Protestant traditions really split over what a verse *means*. The one real argument is about how v. 14 applies to Lent and Easter, covered there.

---

**v. 1**
- Guzik says this date starts one long vision covering chapters 8–11. The vision opens with God's glory at the temple and ends with that glory leaving. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-8/
- Guzik quotes Vawter and Hoppe, who date it to 17 September 592 B.C.E. He also quotes Block: Ezekiel 14:1–3 and 20:1 suggest the elders came regularly to hear a word from God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-8/
- The Pulpit Commentary says news of idolatry in the temple had probably reached the exiles. It also guesses that these elders may have been visitors from Judah, not exiles. It takes "the hand of the Lord" to mean a trance. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-8.html

**v. 2**
- Guzik: this figure is like the human-like picture of God in Ezekiel 1:27. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-8/
- Pulpit: this is a theophany (an appearance of God), like chapter 1. Unlike chapter 1, there are no cherubim and no rainbow, only fire. In its sermon notes, the fire below stands for God's anger at sin and the brightness above for his glory. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-8.html

**v. 3**
- Guzik, citing Feinberg: Ezekiel never really left Babylon. He went to Jerusalem "in spirit" and was brought back in spirit (11:24). Guzik thinks the four scenes are probably not one real-time snapshot. God was showing what was really going on, both outwardly and spiritually. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-8/
- **The idol of jealousy.** Guzik cites Taylor: the idol was an insult to God, so it provoked his jealousy. He traces the history: Manasseh put an idol in the temple, Josiah burned it, and now one was back. Wright notes that the Hebrew word for this idol is used elsewhere only in Deut 4:16 and 2 Chr 33:7, 15. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-8/
- Pulpit: what the idol was is guesswork. It may have been an Asherah pole (like Manasseh's), Baal, Ashtaroth, or even Tammuz. Pulpit also links this gate with the "upper gate" mentioned elsewhere, a busy spot where crowds gathered. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-8.html

**v. 4**
- Guzik: God's glory and the debased idols stand in sharp contrast. God's glory once filled the tabernacle and the temple, but by chapters 10–11 it will be gone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-8/
- Pulpit: Ezekiel had to look at the glory and then at the idol. The contrast between the two shows how guilty Judah was. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-8.html

**v. 5**
- Guzik, citing Taylor: the king used the north gate because the palace stood to the north. So this idol is tied to the royal house. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-8/

**v. 6**
- Guzik: their idolatry was making God choose to leave his own sanctuary. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-8/
- Pulpit: the temple was already like a shrine God had left, and he was coming back now only as Judge. It compares the voice that, according to Josephus, said "Let us depart hence" before Rome destroyed Jerusalem. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-8.html

**vv. 7–8**
- Guzik quotes Block: since this is a vision, we don't need to ask how the digging worked. Guzik's application is that seeing what is really inside can take effort. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-8/
- Pulpit asks how the worshippers got in if Ezekiel had to dig. It suggests the court entrance had been blocked in Josiah's day and the idolaters came in another way. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-8.html
- Matthew Henry: someone had built a wall to hide the rooms. To him that was a shrewd sign that they did something which they had reason to be ashamed of. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/8-8.html

**v. 9**
- Guzik quotes Poole calling these sins loathsome and many. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-8/

**v. 10**
- Guzik cites Feinberg: most interpreters see the animal worship of Egypt here. He links it to Romans 1:23. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-8/
- Pulpit: probably Egyptian animal worship, with the scarab beetle likely prominent. It suggests Judah's political alliances with Pharaoh revived it. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-8.html
- Precept Austin: the carvings break the second commandment (Ex 20:4) and Deut 4:18. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_810-18
- The Layman's Bible Commentary agrees the pictures recall magical paintings in Egypt. It suggests the elders were loyal to God in public while worshipping images in secret. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lbc/ezekiel-8.html

**v. 11**
- **Seventy elders.** Precept Austin contrasts them with the faithful seventy elders who ate before God in Exodus 24. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_810-18
- Pulpit: the number was probably chosen with Exodus 24 in mind, and it is not the later Sanhedrin. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-8.html
- **Jaazaniah.** Guzik quotes Taylor: Shaphan was probably Josiah's secretary, and Jaazaniah was the black sheep of a worthy family. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-8/
- Pulpit: Shaphan's family backed Josiah's reforms and Jeremiah. It says Shaphan's name means "the Lord is listening," which makes the elders' words in v. 12 ironic. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-8.html
- **Incense.** Pulpit: these laymen were acting as priests with incense, which only Aaron's sons could offer. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-8.html Precept Austin contrasts this with the holy incense of the Day of Atonement (Lev 16:13). https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_810-18

**v. 12**
- Guzik: they excused their sin by saying God did not see. In fact they had left God, not the other way round. He quotes Block: what they said about God was false of him, but true of the idols in front of them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-8/
- Pulpit: they saw God as a local god who had walked away. It notes this is the first of several popular sayings Ezekiel quotes in the book. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-8.html

**v. 13**
- Guzik quotes Poole: there's no need to argue about why these later sins are "greater," since all of them are very great. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-8/

**v. 14 (Tammuz)**
- **Who Tammuz was.** Guzik quotes Feinberg: Tammuz was the Babylonian god Dumuzi, Ishtar's lover, the same as the Greek Adonis. This is the only time the Bible names him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-8/
- Pulpit: all interpreters agree he is Adonis, and Jerome said so. The cult marked nature dying and reviving each year, and all guesses about the name's meaning are uncertain. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-8.html
- **Women and where they sat.** Guzik quotes Vawter and Hoppe: Ezekiel probably saw women in the inner court as a profanation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-8/ Gill says the women were out of their proper place, sitting where only kings of David's line could sit. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/8-14.html Ellicott sees a progression across the scenes: the people's image worship, then the elders' creature worship, then the corrupt and debasing rites of their women. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/8-14.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: Instead of weeping for the national sins, they wept for the idol. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/8-14.htm
- **Timing.** Constable notes the vision was in September, perhaps when Tammuz was thought to die. He also mentions the view that "Tammuz" names a type of lament. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/8-14.html
- **Older detail.** Gill lists many guesses about Tammuz (Adonis, Osiris, Bacchus), drawn from Jewish and classical writers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/8-14.html

- **The Lent and Easter debate.** This is the one place where teachers within this tradition openly disagree. One side claims that later church customs came from Tammuz worship:
  - Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) links the festival's eggs and spring celebration to Easter. He says the church took over Tammuz worship, though he admits he isn't sure what God thinks of it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/8-8.html
  - John MacArthur, drawing on Hislop, says Lent came from a 40-day mourning for Tammuz and that Rome merged it with Easter. https://www.gty.org/sermons/1301-C/bible-questions-and-answers-part-5
  - Precept Austin quotes a writer making the same claim about Lent. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_810-18
  - A bible.org article on "Babylonianism" teaches the Semiramis–Tammuz story and ties it to Easter. https://bible.org/seriespage/babylon-seen-scripture-introduction-rev-17-18

  The other side rejects the claim:
  - GotQuestions says the idea that Easter is pagan rests on hearsay, assumptions, and inferences, with no hard evidence. https://www.gotquestions.org/Easter-pagan-holiday.html
  - Catholic Answers (catholic.com) says linking Easter to Ishtar has no basis in history or reality. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/easter-is-not-a-secretly-pagan-holiday

**v. 15**
- The Berean Study Bible notes on Bible Hub say that idolatry left unchecked keeps growing. https://biblehub.com/ezekiel/8-14.htm

**v. 16**
- **Who the 25 men were.** Barnes and Clarke: the heads of the 24 priestly divisions plus the high priest, so they stand for the priests as the seventy stood for the people. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/cjb/ezekiel/8-16.html Pulpit is more careful: Ezekiel does not say they were priests, though the number points that way. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-8.html Gill says it's uncertain whether they were priests or princes, and probably some of both. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/cjb/ezekiel/8-16.html Guzik's summary puts sun worship among the priests. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-8/
- **Backs to the temple.** Pulpit: turning their backs was itself a picture of apostasy (2 Chr 29:6), and the worship looks Persian. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-8.html Barnes: God's seat was placed at the west, perhaps to guard against worship of the rising sun. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/cjb/ezekiel/8-16.html

**v. 17**
- **"Violence."** Barnes: violence means sin against people, and abominations mean sin against God. In Jerusalem the two went together. Ellicott: "returned" means they slid back after Josiah's reforms. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/8-17.htm
- **"The branch to their nose" – (1) a sun-worship ritual.** Pulpit compares Persian worshippers who held twigs while praying to the sun. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-8.html Barnes thinks Ezekiel wrote "nose" instead of "mouth" on purpose, as an insult. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/8-17.html Constable leans this way too, citing Saggs and an Akkadian worship gesture. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/8-17.html
- **(2) A gesture of contempt.** Guzik, citing Feinberg, calls it some unclear expression of contempt for God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-8/ Matthew Henry thinks it may be a saying about mocking God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/8-17.html
- **(3) A scribal correction for "my nose".** In this reading the original said "my nose" and meant a stench in God's face. Gill reports that Jewish tradition lists this as one of 18 scribal corrections. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/8-17.htm Guzik reports that Vawter and Hoppe think the text should read "my nose." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-8/ The NAB, a Catholic translation, reads "my nose." https://biblehub.com/ezekiel/8-17.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed).** Calvin rejects the "my nose" theory. He reads the line as they put forth a branch to their wrath — that is, to their destruction. https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom22/calcom22.xii.xv.html
- **Modern scholarship (NET note, via Precept Austin).** The meaning is unclear. A possible parallel is a Syrian carving of a king holding a flower to his nose while worshipping the stars. https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_810-18
- **Other ideas.** Guzik reports Wright's suggestion that it imitated the Egyptian ankh. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-8/ Jerome, via the Treasury of Scripture Knowledge, explained it as a palm branch used to worship idols. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/bsb/ezekiel/8-17.html

**v. 18**
- Pulpit: this verse leads into chapter 9 and stresses that the judgment will show no pity. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ezekiel-8.html
- Poole: God calls it a "cry," not prayer, like idolaters who think noise gets them heard. He says this doesn't weaken God's mercy to those who truly pray. Instead it should push us to pray with heart, and not only cry loud with voice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/8-18.htm
- Gill: they turned their backs on God, so he turns a deaf ear. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/8-18.html
- The Berean Study Bible notes call this a judicial hardening, when the chance to repent has passed. They link it to Proverbs 1:28. https://biblehub.com/study/ezekiel/8-18.htm
